fetched_contents.text: Safety and effectiveness of a recombinant hepatitis E vaccine in women of childbearing age in rural Bangladesh: a phase 4, double-blind, cluster-randomised, controlled trial Summary Background Hepatitis E virus (HEV) leads to high mortality in pregnant women in low-income countries. We aimed to evaluate the safety of a HEV vaccine and its effectiveness in preventing hepatitis E during pregnancy. Methods In this phase 4, double-blind, cluster-randomised trial, 67 villages in Matlab, Bangladesh, were randomised 1:1 to receive HEV239 (a recombinant HEV vaccine) or a control vaccine (Hepa-B, a hepatitis B vaccine), using block randomisation with random number tables and blocks of size eight, stratified by cluster population size. Eligible non-pregnant women (aged 16–39 years) were vaccinated intramuscularly on day 0, at 1 month, and at 6 months, and followed up for 2 years after the last immunisation. The primary endpoint was hepatitis E in the pregnant, per-protocol population (those who received all three doses within 2 days of the scheduled dates), while safety was a secondary endpoint, assessed in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population (participants who received at least one dose). Solicited adverse events were recorded for the first 7 days after each dose, and unsolicited events until 2 years after a participant's final dose. Pregnancy-related safety outcomes were assessed in the pregnant ITT population. This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT02759991). Findings Between Oct 2, 2017, and Feb 28, 2019, 19 460 participants were enrolled and received either HEV239 (9478 [48·7%] participants, 33 clusters) or Hepa-B (9982 [51·3%] participants, 34 clusters), of whom 17 937 (92·2%) participants received three doses and 17 613 (90·5%) were vaccinated according to protocol (8524 [48·4%] in the HEV239 group and 9089 [51·6%] in the control group). No pregnant participants were confirmed to have hepatitis E in either treatment group. HEV239 showed a mild safety profile, similar to Hepa-B, with no difference in the proportion of solicited adverse events between groups and no severe solicited events. Pain was the most common local symptom (1215 [12·8%] HEV239 recipients and 1218 [12·2%] Hepa-B recipients) and fever the most common systemic symptom (141 [1·5%] HEV239 recipients and 145 [1·5%] Hepa-B recipients). None of the serious adverse events or deaths were vaccine related. Among pregnant participants, the HEV239 group had a higher risk of miscarriage (136 [5·7%] of 2407 pregnant participants) compared with the control group (102 [3·9%] of 2604; adjusted odds ratio 1·54 [95% CI 1·15–2·08]). Interpretation The effectiveness of HEV239 in pregnant women remains uncertain. HEV239 was safe and well tolerated in non-pregnant women, but findings regarding miscarriage warrant further investigation. Funding Research Council of Norway; Innovax. Introduction Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is a major cause of acute viral hepatitis worldwide, causing endemic disease or outbreaks in low-income countries with poor sanitation.1 Clinically, hepatitis caused by HEV resembles other types of acute viral hepatitis and is typically self-limiting.2 Severity increases with age, with a projected 1–3% fatality rate.3 Africa and the Indian subcontinent are the most frequently affected areas.1 Pregnant patients face a high mortality rate of 5–25%, and survivors have high rates of miscarriage (spontaneous abortion) and stillbirth.4,5 HEV infection can also have poor outcomes in patients with chronic liver disease and those who are immunocompromised.6 HEV, a member of the Hepeviridae family, comprises eight genotypes under a single serotype, of which four primarily infect humans.7 HEV1 and HEV2 cause outbreaks in humans, while the zoonotic HEV3 and HEV4 cause sporadic cases in humans. The remaining genotypes (HEV5–8) are predominantly found in animals.8 The recombinant HEV vaccine HEV239 (Hecolin; Xiamen Innovax Biotech, Xiamen, China) underwent a large phase 3 clinical study in China, in which the observed efficacy after three doses was 100% (95% CI 72·1–100·0), and adverse events related to the vaccine were mild.9 HEV239 is developed from HEV1 and showed cross-protection in the Chinese study, wherein HEV4 was prominent. Data are lacking on protection of the vaccine against HEV1–3. To evaluate efficacy against all genotypes that commonly cause illness in humans, further testing in diverse geographical locations is necessary. In south Asia, including Bangladesh, the most common circulating human strain is HEV1.8,10,11 WHO's Strategic Advisory Group of Experts has not recommended the HEV239 vaccine in endemic areas due to several knowledge gaps,12 and has thus called for more research on efficacy and safety in specific populations, such as pregnant women.13,14 Several studies from the south Asian region report high numbers of maternal and neonatal HEV-related deaths, highlighting the need to reduce the burden in this region.15,16 As estimates show that Bangladesh alone has around 1000 HEV-related maternal deaths annually,17 and the epidemiology aligns with other parts of south Asia,15 a trial on HEV239 in Bangladesh would provide relevant results for the estimated 1·5 billion south Asians at risk for HEV infection. fetched_contents.text: Safety of hepatitis E vaccination for pregnancy: a post-hoc analysis of a randomized, double-blind, controlled phase 3 clinical trial ABSTRACT Special attention has been paid to Hepatitis E (HE) prophylaxis for pregnant women due to poor prognosis of HE in this population. We conducted a post-hoc analysis based on the randomized, double-blind, HE vaccine (Hecolin)-controlled phase 3 clinical trial of human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine (Cecolin) conducted in China. Eligible healthy women aged 18–45 years were randomly assigned to receive three doses of Cecolin or Hecolin and were followed up for 66 months. All the pregnancy-related events throughout the study period were closely followed up. The incidences of adverse events, pregnancy complications, and adverse pregnancy outcomes were analysed based on the vaccine group, maternal age, and interval between vaccination and pregnancy onset. During the study period, 1263 Hecolin receivers and 1260 Cecolin receivers reported 1684 and 1660 pregnancies, respectively. The participants in the two vaccine groups showed similar maternal and neonatal safety profiles, regardless of maternal age. Among the 140 women who were inadvertently vaccinated during pregnancy, the incidences of adverse reactions had no statistical difference between the two groups (31.8% vs 35.1%, p = 0.6782). The proximal exposure to HE vaccination was not associated with a significantly higher risk of abnormal foetal loss (OR 0.80, 95% CI 0.38–1.70) or neonatal abnormality (OR 2.46, 95% CI 0.74–8.18) than that to HPV vaccination, as did distal exposure. Significant difference was not noted between pregnancies with proximal and distal exposure to HE vaccination. Conclusively, HE vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy is not associated with increased risks for both the pregnant women and pregnancy outcomes. There are an estimated 20 million HEV infections worldwide every year, leading to approximately 3.3 million symptomatic cases and 44,000 deaths [1]. Although HEV infection is an acute and self-limited disease, progressions to fulminant hepatic failure and other severe consequences have been recorded in pregnant women [2,3]. In some high-prevalence areas, HEV infection has become a major contributor to maternal mortality and abnormal foetal loss [4]. A substantially higher maternal case fatality rate in pregnant women with HEV infection, varied between 3.2% and 70%, was shown in a meta-analysis [5]. Other adverse pregnancy outcomes, including low birth weight, stillbirth, preterm birth (<32 weeks), and intrauterine deaths, were also reported to be highly associated with HEV infection [6]. A recombinant HE vaccine (Hecolin; Xiamen Innovax, Xiamen, China), which has been licensed in 2011 and 2020 in China and Pakistan, separately, is the world’s first and only vaccine to prevent HEV infection. It has been demonstrated with good safety and an efficacy of 100% within 12 months after the third dose in a large-scale, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial [7]. The efficacy of 93.3% (95% confidence interval [CI] 78.6–97.9) in the per-protocol set was confirmed within 4.5 years of follow-up [8]. The highly efficacious HE vaccine may hold great promise for reducing the high mortality and multiple adverse outcomes associated with HEV infection in pregnant women. However, concerns on whether HE vaccination has a causal effect on adverse pregnancy outcomes warrant further investigation in the absence of rigorous data in clinical trials currently. A published post-hoc analysis with a limited sample size of inadvertent HE vaccinees during pregnancy in Hecolin’s phase 3 trial did not show any potential risk for foetus [9]. Therefore, with a view to further investigation of the potential risk posed by HE vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy, we conducted a post-hoc analysis of pregnancy outcomes based on a large-scale phase 3 clinical trial of an Escherichia coli (E. coli)-produced human papillomavirus (HPV) bivalent vaccine, in which the control group received Hecolin. fetched_contents.text: Evaluating the Efficacy and Safety of Hepatitis E Vaccination in Reproductive-Age Women: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis Abstract Background: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection presents a significant health risk in endemic regions, especially for pregnant women, who face higher risks of severe complications, including maternal and fetal mortality. The recombinant HEV vaccine, HEV239, has demonstrated high efficacy in the general population, yet data on its safety and efficacy in women of a childbearing age remain limited. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of HEV239 in this specific population, with a focus on pregnancy-related outcomes. Methods: A comprehensive search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Scopus, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Studies were included if they reported outcomes on HEV239′s safety or efficacy in women of childbearing age, with data being extracted and analyzed for immunogenicity, HEV incidence, and maternal adverse events. The risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane and Newcastle Ottawa Scales, and a random-effects meta-analysis was performed. Results: Three studies, enrolling over 23,000 participants, were included in the current systematic review, with two meeting the criteria for meta-analysis. HEV239 demonstrated high efficacy in preventing hepatitis E infection, with no significant increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes such as stillbirth or elective termination. However, there was an elevated risk of miscarriage (odds ratio [OR], 1.60; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.99–2.57). The analysis revealed high heterogeneity for miscarriage outcomes (I2 = 67%), reflecting variability in study designs and populations. Conclusions: HEV239 is effective in preventing HEV infection among women of childbearing age, although caution is advised when administering the vaccine near conception due to potential miscarriage risks. Future studies should focus on understanding the biological mechanisms and timing-specific safety to guide vaccination recommendations. ## What the evidence says about safety in pregnancy

The current evidence for HEV239 safety during pregnancy is **mixed** and largely based on **human studies** rather than animal/observational evidence alone. The most directly relevant evidence includes a large phase 4 cluster-randomised trial in Bangladesh and a post-hoc analysis of a phase 3 trial, both of which are human studies and therefore more relevant than animal data for pregnancy safety [N1-F1][N1-F2]. This is important because pregnancy-specific pharmacokinetics and placental transfer are not directly provided in the supplied evidence, so the evidence base is weaker on placental transfer and fetal exposure than on adverse outcomes [N2-R2][N2-R3].

### Adverse pregnancy outcomes reported or not reported
The available evidence reports **some adverse pregnancy outcomes**, but not all of them. The Bangladesh phase 4 trial found that **pregnant participants in the HEV239 group had a higher risk of miscarriage** compared with the control group: 5.7% versus 3.9% (adjusted odds ratio 1.54; 95% CI 1.15–2.08) [N1-F1]. The same study also reports **no confirmed hepatitis E infection in pregnant participants** in either group, and no serious adverse events or deaths were vaccine-related [N1-F1].

The post-hoc analysis of a phase 3 trial concludes that **HE vaccination during or shortly before pregnancy is not associated with increased risks for pregnant women or pregnancy outcomes** [N1-R2]. However, this analysis is **post-hoc and based on inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy**, which weakens its ability to establish causality [N1-F2]. It also found that among women inadvertently vaccinated during pregnancy, the incidences of adverse reactions had no statistical difference between groups, and proximal exposure to HE vaccination was not associated with significantly higher risk of abnormal fetal loss or neonatal abnormality [N1-F2].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of HEV239 in reproductive-age women similarly found **no significant increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes such as stillbirth or elective termination**, but **an elevated risk of miscarriage** (OR 1.60; 95% CI 0.99–2.57), with high heterogeneity for miscarriage outcomes (I2 = 67%) [N2-F3]. This suggests that miscarriage is the most consistently reported adverse pregnancy outcome in the evidence, but stillbirth, elective termination, and other outcomes are less consistently reported or not reported at all in some studies [N2-F3].

### Confidence in safety by study design and sample size
Confidence in safety is **graded downward** by study design and sample size. The strongest evidence is from the Bangladesh cluster-randomised trial, which had a very large sample size (19,460 participants) and included both **intention-to-treat** and **per-protocol** analyses [N1-F1]. This trial is therefore more reliable than smaller observational or post-hoc analyses. However, it is still a **cluster-randomised trial**, so it may have less precision than individual-level randomised trials, and its main outcome was based on pregnant participants only, with a relatively small subset of pregnant women in the ITT population (2,407 HEV239 participants and 2,604 control participants) [N1-F1].

The post-hoc analysis of the phase 3 trial is weaker because it is based on **inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy** and a limited sample size of 1,263 Hecolin receivers and 1,260 Cecolin receivers [N1-F2]. It is also a **post-hoc analysis** of a trial originally designed for HPV vaccination, which reduces confidence in the causal inference for HEV239 during pregnancy. The systematic review and meta-analysis is also limited by **heterogeneity** and the fact that only three studies were included, with two meeting the criteria for meta-analysis [N2-F3].

In short, the evidence base is strongest for **safety in non-pregnant women** and weakest for **definitive safety in pregnancy**. The available human studies suggest that HEV239 is generally **well tolerated in pregnant women** with adverse-event rates similar to those in matched non-pregnant women [N1-R5], but they also report **some concern about miscarriage** and recommend caution around conception [N2-F3]. Overall, the confidence in safety is moderate to low, because the evidence is mixed, sample sizes are uneven, and the most concerning adverse outcome—miscarriage—is not fully explained by the studies [N1-F1][N2-F3].

## What the evidence says about potential risks and limitations

### Observed or suspected adverse events linked to vaccination
The evidence points to **one main suspected adverse event** linked to HEV239 vaccination during pregnancy: **miscarriage**. The Bangladesh phase 4 trial found a higher risk of miscarriage in pregnant participants receiving HEV239 compared with control participants [N1-F1]. The systematic review and meta-analysis similarly found an elevated risk of miscarriage (OR 1.60; 95% CI 0.99–2.57) [N2-F3]. The WHO review concluded that the safety signal of spontaneous abortion associated with exposure to Hecolin around the onset of pregnancy **cannot be disregarded**, even though there is **no conclusive evidence** of a safety problem [N5-F4]. It also notes that the Bangladesh study found no increased risk of stillbirth or induced abortion at any of the three exposure periods [N5-F4].

In contrast, the post-hoc analysis of the phase 3 trial found **no statistically significant increase in adverse pregnancy outcomes** among women inadvertently vaccinated during pregnancy, and proximal HE vaccination exposure was not associated with abnormal fetal loss or neonatal abnormality [N1-F2]. However, this result should be interpreted cautiously because the analysis was **post-hoc**, based on a limited sample of inadvertent vaccinees, and the study was originally designed for HPV vaccination [N1-F2].

The WHO review also notes that **no increased risk of spontaneous abortion was found among women who received Hecolin >90 days before pregnancy** [N5-F4]. That is important because it suggests that the timing of vaccination may matter: **early pregnancy** or **very close to conception** may be more concerning than vaccination much earlier before pregnancy [N5-F4].

### Limitations such as lack of long-term follow-up or confounding factors
The evidence is limited by several important weaknesses. First, the Bangladesh trial followed participants for **2 years after the last immunisation**, but the pregnancy-related safety outcomes were assessed only in the pregnant ITT population, and the study did not report long-term follow-up for adverse pregnancy outcomes beyond that time [N1-F1]. That means long-term risks cannot be ruled out from the supplied evidence.

Second, the post-hoc analysis is limited by **inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy**, which introduces **selection bias** because the exposed and unexposed groups may differ in baseline characteristics, and the trial was not originally designed to compare HEV239 with placebo during pregnancy [N1-F2]. The WHO review explicitly acknowledges that **it might be difficult to conduct a large randomized controlled trial** to assess the risk of spontaneous abortion, and therefore the evidence remains inconclusive [N5-F4].

Third, the systematic review and meta-analysis had **high heterogeneity for miscarriage outcomes** (I2 = 67%), reflecting variability in study designs, populations, and outcome definitions [N2-F3]. This means that the pooled result should not be overinterpreted, and individual studies may differ substantially in their findings.

Fourth, there is **confounding** in the Bangladesh trial because **no increased risk of spontaneous abortion was found among women who received Hecolin >90 days before pregnancy**, and the WHO review also considers the possibility that the hepatitis B control vaccine may have a protective effect against spontaneous abortion, though there is no evidence of that effect for hepatitis B vaccines [N5-F4]. This is an important limitation because it means that the observed effect may be **spurious**, **related to other factors**, or **not specific to HEV239**.

### Which populations or doses are most studied and which are understudied
The evidence is **heavily concentrated** on **women of childbearing age**, particularly **pregnant women in Bangladesh** and **inadvertently vaccinated women during pregnancy** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. The Bangladesh trial is the largest and most directly relevant human study, but it focused on **a single population** in rural Bangladesh and used a **3-dose schedule** [N1-F1]. The post-hoc analysis and WHO review also focus on **inadvertent vaccination during pregnancy**, which is not representative of routine vaccination timing [N1-F2][N5-F4].

By contrast, **dose timing and formulation-specific differences** are understudied in the supplied evidence. The WHO review notes that **analysis of the relation between spontaneous abortion and the timing of vaccine administration**, particularly before pregnancy, is needed to determine whether the risk is related to the time very close to conception [N5-F4]. It also recommends analysis of **other vaccine-related adverse events** and **maternal risk factors**, such as age, parity, and prior HEV exposure [N5-F4]. This indicates that the evidence base is thin for **dose-specific safety** and for **vaccine formulations** other than Hecolin/HEV239.

Overall, the supplied evidence is strongest for **women of childbearing age** and **pregnant women in Bangladesh**, but it is **understudied** for **other populations**, **other vaccine formulations**, and **dose timing around conception** [N1-F1][N1-F2][N5-F4]. The most studied dose schedule is the **three-dose schedule**, but the WHO also mentions a **2-dose schedule** as an approved campaign schedule, suggesting that **dose regimens** are an area of ongoing guidance rather than fully established safety evidence [N5-F4].

## What official guidance and recommendations say

### Explicit statements from regulatory agencies or professional societies
The supplied evidence includes two major official statements: the **WHO Hepatitis E vaccines safety Working Group** and the **WHO Strategic Advisory Group of Experts (SAGE)**, plus some broader vaccine-safety context from CDC and other sources [N5-F4][N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N3-R5].

WHO is the most directly relevant authority here. The WHO review states that **the safety signal of spontaneous abortion associated with exposure to Hecolin around the onset of pregnancy cannot be disregarded**, and that **no conclusive evidence of a safety problem with Hecolin® vaccination and spontaneous abortion** has been found, but an increased risk **cannot be excluded** [N5-F4]. WHO also notes that **no increased risk of spontaneous abortion was found among women who received Hecolin® >90 days before pregnancy**, and there was **no difference between the groups in the rates of stillbirth or induced abortion** at any of the three exposure periods [N5-F4].

SAGE concluded that in **fragile, conflict-affected and vulnerable settings** with documented HEV circulation where the risk of severe disease in pregnancy is high, the **benefits of vaccinating women of childbearing age outweigh the potential harms** [N5-F4]. This context is useful because it provides a general framework for interpreting vaccine safety during pregnancy, even though it is not specific to HEV239 [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

### Recommended timing or contraindications during pregnancy
The evidence does **not support routine vaccination during pregnancy**, and the WHO guidance is cautious about timing. WHO also recommends that in outbreak settings, **vaccination should be avoided at the onset of or during early pregnancy**, with a detailed analysis of safety outcomes [N5-F4]. This implies a **cautious recommendation**: if pregnancy occurs around the time of vaccination, the potential risk of spontaneous abortion should be weighed against the benefit of vaccination. However, WHO does not state a strict contraindication in all pregnancies; rather, it emphasizes **avoidance around the onset of or during early pregnancy** and **additional safety assessments** in outbreak settings [N5-F4].

The general vaccine-safety context from CDC and other sources is broader: **live vaccines are contraindicated during pregnancy**, while **inactivated vaccines are generally safe** [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. That general principle is consistent with the HEV239 guidance because HEV239 is a **recombinant subunit vaccine** and therefore likely an **inactivated vaccine** rather than a live vaccine [N2-R4][N5-F4].

The supplied evidence does **not provide country-specific guidance** beyond WHO and SAGE. In summary, official guidance is **cautious rather than outright contraindicative**. General vaccine-safety principles support **inactivated vaccines** over **live vaccines** during pregnancy [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].
